course.title: French from the Beginning
course.description: A progressive introduction to French for learners with no prior knowledge. Lessons introduce sounds and useful words before building short everyday conversations.

lessons.title: French Sound Patterns and First Words
lessons.introduction: Start with a few common French sound patterns and first words. French spelling does not always match English spelling, so listen for whole sound patterns rather than translating letters one at a time.

objectives.title: Notice French sound patterns
objectives.description: Distinguish several common French vowel sounds from familiar English sounds.

objectives.title: Say first French words
objectives.description: Use a simple greeting and say a few first French words aloud.

vocabulary.definition_french: Salutation utilisée pendant la journée.
Salutation familière.
Réponse affirmative.
Réponse négative.
Mot pour exprimer sa gratitude.
D'une manière satisfaisante.
Ce qui est perçu par l'ouïe.
Signe écrit de l'alphabet.

grammar.title: Letters and sounds
grammar.summary: A written letter can have different sounds in French; common letter combinations also represent single sounds.
grammar.explanation_english: Learn a new word as a whole sound-and-spelling unit. The final consonant is often silent, but there are exceptions; do not assume every final letter is silent.

lessons.pronunciation: The French u /y/ is not the same as English oo /u/. Round the lips for /y/ while keeping the tongue forward. The French r /ʁ/ is made at the back of the mouth; a clear approximation is fine at first.

dialogue.title: A first hello
dialogue.english_context: The speakers say hello and exchange a polite response.

exercises.prompt: Choose the French word for “hello” in a polite daytime greeting.
exercises.explanation: Bonjour is the standard daytime greeting.
Merci means “thank you.”
Oui is the affirmative response “yes.”
Salut is an informal hi or bye.

exercises.prompt: Which pair is French u /y/ and English oo /u/?
exercises.explanation: French u is a rounded front vowel, not the English oo vowel.

lessons.recap: You can recognize a few first words, greet someone with bonjour, and remember that spelling and sound do not always match one-to-one.

lessons.title: Greetings and Polite Expressions
lessons.introduction: Use greetings and polite expressions to open and close a short exchange. Choose between a neutral expression and a familiar one according to the situation.

objectives.title: Greet someone politely
objectives.description: Choose a suitable greeting and respond to a simple how-are-you question.

objectives.title: Use polite expressions
objectives.description: Use please, thank you, and goodbye in a short exchange.

vocabulary.definition_french: Salutation utilisée pendant la journée.
Salutation utilisée le soir.
Formule pour prendre congé.
Formule de politesse pour demander quelque chose.
Formule familière pour demander quelque chose.
Mot pour s'excuser ou demander de répéter.

vocabulary.translation: how are you?; it is going
vocabulary.definition_french: Question ou réponse familière sur l'état d'une personne.
Adverbe qui augmente l'intensité.

grammar.title: Choosing a polite expression
grammar.summary: Use s'il vous plaît in a formal or plural situation and s'il te plaît with one person you address informally.
grammar.explanation_english: The pronouns vous and te signal different ways of addressing someone. When unsure in a service interaction, s'il vous plaît is a safe polite choice.

lessons.pronunciation: In bonsoir and au revoir, pronounce the final r as the French sound /ʁ/. Keep the rhythm smooth and do not add a vowel or extra syllable after it.

dialogue.title: A polite greeting
dialogue.context: A customer greets a café worker and makes a simple request.
dialogue.english_context: A short service encounter using a polite greeting and please.

turns.french_text: Très bien, merci. Un café, s'il vous plaît.
turns.english_translation: Very well, thank you. A coffee, please.

exercises.explanation: Bonsoir is used as an evening greeting.

exercises.prompt: Choose the polite “please” for a service interaction.
exercises.explanation: S'il vous plaît is the formal or plural form.
Au revoir is a common way to say goodbye.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase asks informally how someone is?
exercises.explanation: Ça va? is a familiar “How are you?”
S'il te plaît is used with one person addressed informally.

lessons.recap: You can open and close a polite exchange and choose a suitable please expression. Use bonsoir in the evening and au revoir when leaving.

lessons.title: Introducing Yourself
lessons.introduction: Learn to give your name and ask another person's name. The useful patterns are short: je m'appelle for a name and comment vous vous appelez for a polite question.

objectives.title: Say your name
objectives.description: Introduce yourself and ask another person their name using a short memorized phrase.

objectives.title: Recognize basic identity words
objectives.description: Understand common words for a name and a person in a simple introduction.

vocabulary.definition_french: Pronom sujet de la première personne du singulier.
Pronom sujet pour une personne vouvoyée ou plusieurs personnes.
Avoir un nom; verbe pronominal.
Nom personnel donné à la naissance ou à l'usage.
Mot qui identifie une personne ou une chose, notamment le nom de famille.
Formule de politesse lors d'une première rencontre.
Formule de politesse lors d'une première rencontre.
Adverbe interrogatif sur la manière ou l'identité.

grammar.title: Introducing yourself with s'appeler
grammar.summary: Use je m'appelle to give your name and comment vous appelez-vous to ask someone politely.
grammar.explanation_english: S'appeler is a pronominal verb. The pronoun changes with the subject; this lesson practices je and vous as fixed beginner phrases.

lessons.pronunciation: In je m'appelle, the e in je is often reduced in natural speech, but beginners may pronounce it clearly. Keep the two l sounds in appelle together rather than adding an extra syllable.

dialogue.title: Meeting someone
dialogue.english_context: They exchange names and say pleased to meet you.

turns.french_text: Bonjour, je m'appelle Léa. Et vous ?
turns.english_translation: Hello, my name is Léa. And you?

exercises.prompt: Choose the French phrase for “My name is Léa.”
exercises.explanation: Je m'appelle Léa means “My name is Léa.”
Le prénom means first name.

exercises.prompt: Choose the polite question “What is your name?”
exercises.explanation: Comment vous appelez-vous? asks someone's name politely.

exercises.prompt: What does enchanté mean in a first meeting?
exercises.explanation: Enchanté is a polite “pleased to meet you.”

exercises.prompt: Which pronoun means formal or plural “you”?
exercises.explanation: Vous is formal singular or plural “you.”

lessons.recap: You can give your name with je m'appelle and ask another person's name politely. Enchanté or enchantée is a courteous first-meeting response.

lessons.title: Numbers, Age and Basic Questions
lessons.introduction: Use a few numbers and question words to exchange basic personal information. In French, age is expressed with avoir: j'ai vingt ans, literally “I have twenty years.”

objectives.title: Recognize common numbers
objectives.description: Recognize the numbers zéro, un, deux, trois, and dix in short phrases.

objectives.title: Ask and answer about age
objectives.description: Ask someone's age and give a simple age using avoir.

vocabulary.definition_french: Nombre qui représente une quantité nulle.
Nombre cardinal ou article indéfini masculin.
Nombre cardinal qui suit un.
Nombre cardinal qui suit deux.
Nombre cardinal qui suit neuf.
Expression interrogative sur l'âge.
Posséder ou exprimer certains états.
Période de douze mois.

grammar.title: Numbers zéro through dix
grammar.summary: Learn the French number words from zero to ten as complete spoken and written forms.
grammar.explanation_english: The numbers are zéro (zero), un (one), deux (two), trois (three), quatre (four), cinq (five), six (six), sept (seven), huit (eight), neuf (nine), and dix (ten). Un is also the masculine indefinite article.

grammar.title: Age with avoir
grammar.summary: French uses avoir rather than être to state age: j'ai vingt ans.
grammar.explanation_english: Use avoir + number + ans to say someone's age. The French construction literally says “I have ... years.”

grammar.title: Simple questions
grammar.summary: French questions can use a question word, rising intonation, or inversion in more formal patterns.
grammar.explanation_english: Quel âge avez-vous? uses a question phrase and subject-verb inversion. In conversation, intonation can also form a question; choose a pattern appropriate to the situation.

lessons.pronunciation: The final consonant in dix is usually silent before a pause, but liaison may make it audible before a following vowel. Learn the number as a spoken unit.

dialogue.title: Asking someone's age
dialogue.context: A learner asks another person a basic personal question.
dialogue.english_context: They exchange a name and age politely.

exercises.prompt: Which French verb is used to express age?
exercises.explanation: French uses avoir for age: j'ai vingt ans.
Deux means two.

exercises.prompt: Choose the French question “How old are you?”
exercises.explanation: Quel âge avez-vous? is the polite age question.

exercises.prompt: Complete the age phrase: J'___ vingt ans.
exercises.explanation: The correct first-person form of avoir is ai.
Dix means ten.

lessons.recap: You can recognize introductory numbers and ask someone's age. State age with avoir + number + ans, not être.

lessons.title: Articles and Noun Gender
lessons.introduction: French nouns have grammatical gender. Learn each noun together with its article: un or le for masculine nouns, une or la for feminine nouns. Gender is a grammatical feature, not a statement about a person's identity.

objectives.title: Recognize basic articles
objectives.description: Identify un, une, le, and la in short noun phrases.

objectives.title: Learn nouns with gender
objectives.description: Remember a new French noun together with its article and grammatical gender.

vocabulary.definition_french: Objet composé de pages imprimées ou écrites.
vocabulary.teaching_note: Learn the article with the noun.

vocabulary.definition_french: Meuble avec un plateau et des pieds.
vocabulary.teaching_note: Learn the article with the noun.

vocabulary.definition_french: Boisson ou établissement où l'on sert des boissons.
Bâtiment où l'on habite.
Personne avec qui l'on a une relation d'affection.
Personne avec qui l'on a une relation d'affection.
Instrument qui sert à écrire.
Panneau qui ferme une ouverture.

grammar.title: Articles and grammatical gender
grammar.summary: French nouns are masculine or feminine. The indefinite articles are un and une; the singular definite articles are le and la.
grammar.explanation_english: Learn the article as part of the noun entry because noun gender is not reliably predictable from meaning alone. Before a vowel or mute h, le and la elide to l'.

lessons.pronunciation: Before a vowel sound, le and la elide to l', as in l'ami and l'amie. Un has a nasal vowel; its final n is not pronounced as a separate consonant. Une has a different vowel sound.

dialogue.title: Identifying objects
dialogue.context: Two learners identify simple classroom objects.
dialogue.english_context: They use c'est with masculine and feminine nouns.

exercises.explanation: Livre is masculine: un livre or le livre.
Table is feminine: une table.

exercises.prompt: Which singular definite article is masculine?
exercises.explanation: Le is the masculine singular definite article.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for “the house.”
exercises.explanation: Maison is feminine: la maison.

exercises.prompt: What is the best way to learn a French noun?
exercises.explanation: Learning the article together with the noun helps retain its grammatical gender.

lessons.recap: French nouns have grammatical gender. Learn un/une or le/la together with each noun; never infer a person's identity from a noun's grammatical gender.

lessons.title: Subject Pronouns and Être
lessons.introduction: Use subject pronouns with être to say who someone is or describe a simple state. Être is irregular, so learn its present forms as a small set.

objectives.title: Use être in the present
objectives.description: Choose a basic present form of être with je, tu, il, elle, nous, or vous.

objectives.title: Recognize subject pronouns
objectives.description: Identify common French subject pronouns in short sentences.

vocabulary.definition_french: Pronom sujet de la première personne du singulier.
Pronom sujet pour une personne tutoyée.
Pronom sujet masculin de la troisième personne.
Pronom sujet féminin de la troisième personne.
Pronom sujet de la première personne du pluriel.
Pronom sujet pour une personne vouvoyée ou plusieurs personnes.
Verbe qui exprime notamment l'identité ou l'état.
Personne qui suit des études.
Personne qui suit des études.

grammar.title: Subject pronouns and être
grammar.summary: A French sentence usually has a subject pronoun before the verb. Être is irregular: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont.
grammar.explanation_english: Use the form of être that agrees with the subject. This lesson focuses on common singular forms and vous êtes; the full present paradigm is included in the verb reference.

lessons.pronunciation: The initial s in suis is pronounced; the final s in suis is silent before a pause, as are the final s in es and t in est. Êtes has a clear ê vowel; do not omit its circumflex in writing.

dialogue.title: A simple introduction
dialogue.context: Two people introduce themselves and say where they are.
dialogue.english_context: They use subject pronouns and present forms of être.

exercises.explanation: The first-person singular present form is suis.
Tu is informal singular “you.”
The present form used with vous is êtes.
Nous means “we.”

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence for “She is here.”
exercises.explanation: Elle est ici uses elle with the third-person singular form est.

lessons.recap: Subject pronouns identify who is doing or being. Être has irregular present forms; connect each pronoun with its matching form.

lessons.title: Avoir and Talking About Possessions
lessons.introduction: Use avoir to talk about what someone has. It is also used in a few common expressions, including age. Practice the present forms with simple objects and people.

objectives.title: Use avoir in the present
objectives.description: Use j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, and vous avez in short statements.

objectives.title: Describe a possession
objectives.description: Ask and answer whether someone has a familiar object.

vocabulary.definition_french: Posséder ou exprimer certains états.
Appareil qui permet de communiquer à distance.
Objet qui sert à ouvrir ou fermer une serrure.
Contenant souple pour transporter des objets.
Garçon ou homme qui a les mêmes parents qu'une personne.
Fille ou femme qui a les mêmes parents qu'une personne.
Adverbe qui ajoute un élément.
Préposition qui marque l'accompagnement.

grammar.title: Avoir in the present
grammar.summary: The common present forms are j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.
grammar.explanation_english: Avoir is irregular. The final consonants of many singular forms are not pronounced before a pause; the spelling still changes with the subject.

grammar.title: Negation with ne...pas
grammar.summary: In a simple present-tense statement, ne or n' and pas surround the conjugated verb.
grammar.explanation_english: Place ne before the conjugated verb and pas after it. Use n' instead of ne before a vowel sound: je n'ai pas. With avoir, un, une, and des usually become de (or d' before a vowel) after pas: je n'ai pas de clé. In everyday speech, ne is often omitted, but it is retained in standard written French.
examples: I do not have a key.

lessons.pronunciation: In j'ai, the apostrophe marks elision of je before a vowel. Avoir forms have several different vowel sounds; say each complete form rather than applying a regular verb pattern.

dialogue.title: Do you have a phone?
dialogue.context: Two friends ask about everyday items.
dialogue.english_context: A short question and answer with avoir.

turns.english_translation: Do you have a key too?

turns.french_text: Non, je n'ai pas de clé.
turns.english_translation: No, I do not have a key.

exercises.explanation: The first-person singular present form is ai.
The third-person singular form is a.
Une clé means a key.
Avec means “with.”

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: J'ai un téléphone.
exercises.explanation: J'ai means “I have.”

lessons.recap: Avoir expresses possession and age. Match its irregular present forms to the subject, and learn each object with its article.

lessons.title: Family and Personal Information
lessons.introduction: Use familiar family words and simple possessives to share basic personal information. The words mon, ma, and mes agree with the noun that follows.

objectives.title: Name close family members
objectives.description: Recognize and use common words for family members in a short description.

objectives.title: Share basic information
objectives.description: Give a simple sentence about a family member using a possessive adjective.

vocabulary.definition_french: Ensemble de personnes liées notamment par la parenté.
Femme qui a un enfant.
Homme qui a un enfant.
Garçon ou homme qui a les mêmes parents qu'une personne.
Fille ou femme qui a les mêmes parents qu'une personne.
Le père et la mère d'une personne.
Adjectif possessif de la première personne du singulier.
Adjectif possessif féminin de la première personne du singulier.
Adjectif possessif de la première personne du singulier devant un nom pluriel.
Adjectif possessif féminin de la deuxième personne du singulier.

grammar.title: Possessives mon, ma, mes, and ta
grammar.summary: Mon, ma, and mes mean “my”; ta means informal singular “your.” Possessives agree with the noun that follows.
grammar.explanation_english: Use mon with a masculine singular noun, ma with a feminine singular noun, and mes with a plural noun. Use ta with a feminine singular noun when addressing someone informally. Before a vowel sound, mon is used with a feminine noun: mon amie.

lessons.pronunciation: The final n in mon is normally linked smoothly to the following noun. Do not pronounce the s in les before a pause; it may be heard in liaison before a vowel.

dialogue.title: Talking about family
dialogue.context: A learner asks about another person's family.
dialogue.english_context: The speakers name siblings and use possessives.

turns.french_text: Tu as des frères et sœurs ?
turns.english_translation: Do you have brothers and sisters?

turns.french_text: Oui. J'ai un frère et une sœur.
turns.english_translation: Yes. I have a brother and a sister.

exercises.explanation: La mère means mother.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for “my brother.”
exercises.explanation: Frère is masculine, so use mon frère.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for “my sister.”
exercises.explanation: Sœur is feminine, so use ma sœur.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for “my parents.”
exercises.explanation: Parents is plural, so use mes: mes parents.

exercises.prompt: Complete the informal phrase for “your sister”: ___ sœur.
exercises.explanation: Sœur is feminine singular, so use ta when addressing someone informally.

lessons.recap: You can name close family members and use mon, ma, and mes for “my,” plus ta for informal “your.” The possessive agrees with the noun, not the speaker.

lessons.title: Everyday Activities and Common Verbs
lessons.introduction: Talk about a small number of everyday activities with common present-tense verbs. Regular -er verbs provide a useful pattern, while être, avoir, aller, and faire need special attention.

objectives.title: Describe a simple routine
objectives.description: Use a familiar present-tense verb in a short sentence about an everyday activity.

objectives.title: Recognize common verb forms
objectives.description: Recognize common present-tense verbs and the regular -er pattern in familiar sentences.

vocabulary.definition_french: Utiliser une langue pour communiquer.
Avoir son domicile dans un lieu.
Éprouver de l'affection ou apprécier.
Se déplacer vers un lieu.
Réaliser ou créer quelque chose.
Exercer une activité professionnelle ou une tâche.
Première partie de la journée.
Le jour présent.

grammar.title: Common present-tense verbs
grammar.summary: Many -er verbs use -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent endings; aller, faire, être, and avoir are irregular and should be learned separately.
grammar.explanation_english: For regular -er verbs, the written endings are consistent, though several are silent in speech. Aller and faire do not follow this pattern; use their individual forms.

lessons.pronunciation: The endings -e, -es, and -ent of many regular -er verbs are silent. The nous and vous endings are usually audible; listen for the verb stem and subject together.

dialogue.title: A simple routine
dialogue.context: Two learners talk about where they live and what they do.
dialogue.english_context: They use common present-tense verbs in short sentences.

turns.french_text: Oui, je parle un peu français.
turns.english_translation: Yes, I speak a little French.

exercises.explanation: Habiter means to live or reside.
The nous form of regular parler is parlons.
Aller means to go.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about regular -er verb endings is accurate?
exercises.explanation: Several written endings are silent in speech, especially -e, -es, and -ent.
options: Every ending is pronounced as a separate syllable.

exercises.explanation: Aujourd'hui means today.

lessons.recap: You can describe a simple activity or place using common verbs. Regular -er verbs share a pattern, while frequent verbs such as aller and faire are irregular.

lessons.title: Shopping, Ordering and Everyday Conversations
lessons.introduction: Bring greetings, polite requests, numbers, and familiar objects together in a short shop or café exchange. A simple request with je voudrais is polite and useful.

objectives.title: Make a simple polite request
objectives.description: Order or ask for a familiar item using je voudrais and s'il vous plaît.

objectives.title: Follow a short service exchange
objectives.description: Recognize a greeting, item, price question, and thank-you in a basic interaction.

vocabulary.definition_french: Formule polie pour exprimer un souhait.
Adverbe interrogatif sur la quantité ou le prix.
Valeur monétaire d'un bien ou d'un service.
Liquide transparent nécessaire à la vie.
Viennoiserie faite d'une pâte levée feuilletée, souvent en forme de croissant.
Liste des plats et boissons proposés dans un restaurant.
Donner de l'argent en échange d'un bien ou service.
Somme à payer dans un restaurant.

examples.french_text: Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english_translation: I would like a croissant, please.
How much does the water cost?

grammar.title: Polite requests with je voudrais
grammar.summary: Je voudrais + noun is a polite way to say “I would like ...”. Add s'il vous plaît to make a request courteous.
grammar.explanation_english: Je voudrais uses the conditional form of vouloir as a polite fixed expression. At this beginner level, learn it as a complete phrase rather than deriving the full conditional.
examples: Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
I would like a croissant, please.
How much does the water cost?

lessons.pronunciation: In voudrais, pronounce the oi spelling like /wa/. In l'eau and l'addition, the apostrophe shows that le or la is shortened before a vowel sound.

dialogue.title: At the bakery
dialogue.context: A customer orders a pastry and asks the price.
dialogue.english_context: They greet one another, make a polite request, and close the exchange.

turns.french_text: Bonjour. Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
turns.english_translation: Hello. I would like a croissant, please.

turns.french_text: Non, merci. Combien coûte le croissant ?
turns.english_translation: No, thank you. How much does the croissant cost?

exercises.prompt: Choose the polite way to say “I would like a croissant.”
exercises.explanation: Je voudrais is a polite fixed expression meaning “I would like.”

exercises.prompt: What does combien mean in a price question?
exercises.explanation: Combien asks how much or how many.

exercises.prompt: What does l'addition mean in a restaurant?
exercises.explanation: L'addition is the bill.
S'il vous plaît is the polite request expression.
Un croissant is a croissant.

lessons.recap: You can greet a service worker, make a polite request, ask a price, thank someone, and say goodbye. Keep je voudrais as a complete useful expression.
